title: latency-aware-batching-presets-and-rationale-draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working draft proposing a compact set of latency-aware presets for batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization that product and solutions teams can use as starting points for common SLO buckets (low-latency, balanced, throughput-first). The goal is to reduce the time teams spend tuning per-workload and to standardize the tradeoffs used in cost spreadsheets. This memo focuses on heuristics and rationale rather than final numbers — numbers are proposals to validate in the next sprint.

Context and motivation:
- We repeatedly see teams re-derive similar settings for different models and workloads. A small set of well-documented presets (with clear assumptions) will speed onboarding and make cost estimates more consistent.
- Presets should be conservative (safe defaults) but include explicit knobs and clear expected effects on latency, p95, and unit cost.
- Presets must map directly to columns in the cost model spreadsheet so that engineers can flip between presets and see estimated cost/latency immediately.

Assumptions (apply unless stated):
- Baseline infra: single-GPU serving instance (A100 equivalent) with continuous batching enabled in the runtime.
- Typical request distribution: 60% short (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64–256), 10% long (>256).
- Model families: "compact" (<=13B), "medium" (~13–30B), "large" (>30B). Quantization support differs by family.
- Target SLOs: low-latency p95 <= 100ms, balanced p95 <= 300ms, throughput p95 <= 700ms.

Presets (high-level):
1) low-latency (interactive UI / autosuggest): prioritize p95 and tail latency, accept higher per-token cost.
- batch_strategy: immediate-forwarding (no long aggregation), progressive-bursting enabled (allow small micro-batches up to 4 requests), max_batch_size: 4 for compact, 2 for medium, 1 for large.
- batching_timeout_ms: 6ms for compact, 8ms for medium, 12ms for large.
- prefix_cache: enabled for exact-prefix reuse only, TTL: short (1–5s), cache_key: (model, customer_id, prompt_hash_first_64).
- kv_cache_shard_reuse: best-effort, do not wait to rehydrate across cold starts.
- quantization: prefer fp16 or q8_0 for compact, avoid 4-bit on medium/large unless validated.
- expected impact: p95 improves significantly vs unbatched; cost per token increases 5–20% due to smaller batches.

2) balanced (default recommendation for mixed workloads): balance latency and cost.
- batch_strategy: latency-aware batching with adaptive window.
- max_batch_size: 16 (compact), 8 (medium), 4 (large).
- batching_timeout_ms: 20ms (compact), 30ms (medium), 40ms (large).
- prefix_cache: enabled with prefix clustering (group similar prefixes by hash radius), TTL: 30s–2m.
- kv_cache_shard_reuse: aggressive for same-customer flows, rehydrate asynchronously on miss.
- quantization: q8_0 or q4f16 for compact; q8 for medium; run quick regression eval before enabling on large.
- expected impact: 2–4x better cost/token vs low-latency, modest p95 increases within target.

3) throughput-first (ingestion batch jobs, summarization, embedding-heavy): maximize tokens/sec and reduce $/token.
- batch_strategy: fixed-batch aggregator with large windows and auto-scaling triggers.
- max_batch_size: 64+ (compact), 32 (medium), 16 (large) depending on memory headroom.
- batching_timeout_ms: 100–500ms (configurable by workload).
- prefix_cache: full-query caching (where semantics allow), TTL: minutes to hours.
- kv_cache_shard_reuse: persistent pinned caches for hot-keys.
- quantization: 4-bit (q4f16 or q3_k variants) for compact and medium when quality checks pass; large models should be evaluated carefully.
- expected impact: 5–10x cost reduction vs low-latency; p95 may exceed interactive thresholds.

Practical heuristics and example mappings to spreadsheet columns:
- spreadsheet columns expected (use these names for downstream tooling): 
  - workload_id, workload_name, p95_target_ms, avg_seq_len, short_pct, med_pct, long_pct, preferred_preset, model_family, max_batch_size, batching_timeout_ms, cache_strategy, cache_ttl_s, quantization_profile, est_tokens_per_second, est_cost_per_token_usd, est_monthly_cost_usd, notes
- mapping examples (one-row text examples):
  - chat-widget: p95_target_ms=150, avg_seq_len=48, preferred_preset=balanced, model_family=compact, max_batch_size=16, batching_timeout_ms=20, cache_strategy=prefix_cluster, cache_ttl_s=60, quantization_profile=q8_0
  - realtime-suggestions: p95_target_ms=50, avg_seq_len=16, preferred_preset=low-latency, model_family=compact, max_batch_size=4, batching_timeout_ms=6, cache_strategy=exact-prefix, cache_ttl_s=2, quantization_profile=fp16
  - nightly-indexer: p95_target_ms=1000, avg_seq_len=512, preferred_preset=throughput, model_family=medium, max_batch_size=32, batching_timeout_ms=200, cache_strategy=full-query, cache_ttl_s=3600, quantization_profile=q4f16

Cache recommendations (detailed):
- Prefix vs full-query: prefer prefix caching for interactive where partial reuse is common (chat, autocomplete). Full-query caching is only safe for idempotent workloads where the exact input maps to cached output semantics (embeddings, reranking).
- Cache key design: include model/version, quantization_profile, customer_tier, and normalized prompt prefix. Avoid including transient metadata (timestamps, request ids).
- TTL guidance: short TTLs (1–10s) for high-frequency interactive features where freshness matters; medium TTLs (30s–5m) for session-scoped data; long TTLs (m–h) for bulk/embeddings.
- Warm-up/rehydration: for reclaimed KV cache entries, have an async rehydrate pipeline that primes caches for high-value customers when load is predicted.

Quantization guidance (practical):
- Profiles to include in the spreadsheet: fp16, q8_0, q8_1 (lower perf), q4f16, q3_k (experimental).
- Default enablement: fp16 or q8_0 for compact and medium models unless evals show >1% ROUGE/EM drop for critical tasks.
- Quality gates: integrate a quick eval harness (10–20 prompt sets) into the rollout plan. If any metric regresses >2% relative to fp16 baseline, block auto-enable.
- Rollout plan: canary quantization per-customer_id, measure output divergence and user-facing metrics, then ramp to broader population.

Adaptive strategies and novel knobs (to explore):
- progressive-batching: start serving small micro-batches for tail avoidance and gradually increase batch size as queue depth rises (helps keep p95 down while recovering cost benefits at higher load).
- cache-first routing: for requests where prefix cache hit probability > threshold, route to a lightweight cache-serving tier to return results immediately without invoking full runtime (saves GPU cycles).
- quantization-fallback routing: if quantized model latency or quality is outside thresholds, automatically route to fp16 model variant for that request path and flag in logs.

Experimentation checklist (for validation run):
- baseline capture: collect per-route stats for 2 weeks: per-request seq_len, raw tokens, p50/p95/p99 latency, success/error, cache hit rate, cost per token by model.
- spreadsheet sweep: for each candidate route, run a parameter sweep across max_batch_size [1,4,8,16,32], batching_timeout_ms [5,20,50,200], cache_ttl_s [1,10,60,600], quant_profile [fp16,q8_0,q4f16] and record estimated cost/latency.
- quality eval: run 200 prompt set comparisons for each quantization_profile; store divergence metrics and flag regressions.
- production canary: pick 5–10% traffic split per-route to validate recommended preset for 48–72 hours.

Cost-sheet tips (to standardize across PRs):
- Always show relative delta vs baseline (baseline = fp16, no caching, immediate batching) so reviewers can quickly see benefits.
- Include assumptions block: model weights, GPU SKU, token pricing, and expected concurrency.
- Add an uncertainty column in the sheet for any numbers derived from simulation rather than production.

Open questions / tradeoffs we still need to validate:
- How aggressive can we be enabling 4-bit quant on medium-sized models without unexpected hallucination increases? Needs targeted eval.
- What is the best production metric to gate prefix-TTL reductions (strict freshness vs cost)? Should be business-case dependent.
- SRE implications: large batching windows can interact poorly with autoscaling signals; recommend pause autoscale on canaries.

Next steps (owners and rough timeline):
- Aisha: implement spreadsheet templates and sweep harness (2 weeks).
- Marco: implement progressive-batching prototype in runtime and a small stress test (3 weeks).
- Jing: run quantization regression harness and propose pass/fail thresholds (2 weeks).
- Thomas: coordinate canary test plans with SRE and list safety checks (1 week).

Appendix: quick cheat table (proposed defaults)
- low-latency: max_batch_size={compact:4, medium:2, large:1}, batching_timeout_ms={6,8,12}, cache_ttl_s=1-5, quant=fp16/q8_0
- balanced: max_batch_size={compact:16, medium:8, large:4}, batching_timeout_ms={20,30,40}, cache_ttl_s=30-120, quant=q8_0/q4f16
- throughput: max_batch_size={compact:64+, medium:32, large:16}, batching_timeout_ms=100-500, cache_ttl_s=600-3600, quant=q4f16/q3_k-experimental

Notes: this is a working draft — the purpose is to create a minimal, testable set of presets that teams can adopt quickly and iterate on. Feedback welcome (especially from runtime and SRE) on edge cases (cold starts, autoscale interactions, multi-tenant cache isolation).

-- Aisha
